opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think they're among the great scientific documents of the twentieth century, and they're underappreciated precisely because they look so homely. Piaget was watching his own three children, Jacqueline, Lucienne, and Laurent, and writing down in enormous detail what they did, day after day. That's not how we do developmental psychology now. We run controlled experiments with dozens of babies. But what's remarkable is how many of those observations hold up. If you go and replicate them, the babies really do the things Piaget said they did.

The famous example is the A-not-B error. You hide a toy under one cloth, the baby finds it a few times, then you hide it under a second cloth right in front of them, and the nine-month-old goes right back to the first place. That's been replicated hundreds of times. It's one of the most robust findings in all of psychology, and it came out of a father playing with his kid on the living room floor.

Where Piaget went wrong was more in the interpretation than in the observation. He thought the babies' behavior showed that they didn't yet have a concept of a permanent object. What we've learned since, partly with techniques like looking-time measures, is that babies know a lot more than their actions reveal. The limitation is often in executing the action, in inhibiting a habit, rather than in what they understand. So Piaget underestimated babies. He thought they started with very little and constructed everything through action.

But the deep idea, that children are actively constructing their picture of the world, that they're little scientists, experimenting and revising, I think that's exactly right. That's the idea my own work builds on. We just think they start with more, and that they learn in a more rational, more Bayesian way than he could have formalized at the time.

And there's a methodological lesson too. Piaget was a naturalist. He'd been studying mollusks as a teenager, and he looked at babies with the same patient, careful eye. I think developmental psychology lost something when it moved entirely to the lab. Some of the most interesting things children do, the pretend play, the spontaneous exploration, you only really see if you spend a lot of time just watching them.

r002.rationale: It says Piaget’s observations hold up and that researchers can replicate them, including the A-not-B error.

r003.rationale: It says babies know more than their actions reveal, but does not characterize their cognition as more abstract than Piaget believed.

r004.rationale: It describes children as little scientists who experiment and revise, but does not clearly characterize their mental representations as more theory-like than Piaget believed.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the observations themselves have held up remarkably well, and that's the part of Piaget that people tend to underrate. He was an extraordinary observer. Those early books, where he's essentially keeping a diary of his own three children, Jacqueline and Lucienne and Laurent, are still full of things that we go back and find are true. A baby hiding an object and then looking for it in the wrong place, a baby doing the same action over and over with slight variations as if running a little experiment, the way a one-year-old will start to use a stick to pull something closer. Those descriptions are accurate. If you sit down with a nine-month-old today, you'll see exactly what he saw.

What hasn't held up as well is the interpretation he put on top of them. Piaget thought infants were starting from almost nothing, that they were essentially sensorimotor creatures who only gradually constructed concepts like objects or causality or other minds over the first two years. And the big revolution in my field, starting in the eighties with people like Liz Spelke and Renée Baillargeon, was discovering that if you use methods that don't depend on babies reaching and coordinating their hands, looking-time methods for instance, babies know a great deal more a great deal earlier than he thought. So he underestimated the competence, partly because his measures were tied to what a baby could do with its body.

But I'd say even there he was right about something deep, which is that children are actively constructing knowledge rather than passively absorbing it. He called himself a genetic epistemologist, not a psychologist, and that's the right way to read him. He was asking how knowledge is possible, and he looked at babies to find out. That framing, the child as a little scientist revising theories in the light of evidence, is the one I've spent my career working within, even when the details have changed a lot. So I think of him the way a physicist might think of Newton. The specific mechanism was wrong in important ways, but the questions and the observations are permanent.

r002.rationale: It says the observations have held up, describes them as accurate, and says we can see exactly what Piaget saw in babies today.

r003.rationale: It says infants know more, and know it earlier, than Piaget thought, but does not clearly state that their cognition is more abstract.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re extraordinary. Piaget was a remarkably careful observer, and if you go back to his descriptions of what his own children were doing, you can still find things that suggest experiments we ought to be doing now. He had this wonderful eye for the small, apparently mundane thing a baby does that reveals a really interesting intellectual problem.

I’d distinguish those observations from his larger theoretical picture. We’ve learned that babies know much more, and can learn much more, than his theories sometimes allowed. In particular, if you give children a task that doesn’t require them to coordinate a whole series of actions, you often discover understanding that his tasks missed.

But his fundamental idea—that children are actively trying to figure out how the world works, that they’re constructing and revising their understanding rather than just passively taking things in—that’s still central. And the observations themselves remain a tremendous source of inspiration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the observations are still extraordinary. Piaget was a wonderful observer of children, and if you go back and read those books, you find phenomena that people are still trying to explain. He took very seriously things that most adults would just overlook—what a baby does when you hide an object, or how a child repeats an action with a slight variation.

I think he was much less successful at explaining those observations. In particular, he underestimated how much babies know, partly because his tasks required them to do things that were difficult for reasons other than a lack of understanding. And the idea that development proceeds through these very general, sharply defined stages hasn’t held up very well.

But the fundamental insight—that children’s apparently peculiar behavior reflects an attempt to understand the world—is enormously important. He made children’s thinking a subject worthy of serious scientific investigation.
